# Text and encoding

<!-- Generated by `npm run train` from the sources each rule cites. To change a rule for good, change its source or say so in training/feedback.md; the next training run regenerates this file. -->

- **Decode untrusted or external bytes as text with a strict UTF-8 encoding that throws on invalid bytes, such as `new UTF8Encoding(false, throwOnInvalidBytes: true)` or the codebase's shared strict encoding, not `Encoding.UTF8`.** `Encoding.UTF8` quietly swaps invalid bytes for replacement characters. That hides corrupt input, and the code carries on with the wrong content. *Check:* Look for `Encoding.UTF8.GetString`, `[Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetString` or a default-encoding reader used on request bodies, remote responses, files supplied by users or other untrusted bytes. *Note:* Committed test fixtures don't count as untrusted input. See the rule below on what not to report. <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; project-template outcomes of #331</sub>
- **Don't call a text API overload that takes no encoding and so picks one implicitly. Always pass an explicit strict UTF-8 encoding. For example, pass `contentEncoding` set to the shared strict UTF-8 encoding to every `Results.Content`, `Results.Text`, `TypedResults.Content` and `TypedResults.Text` call, including calls in test-only hosts.** An implicit or framework-default encoding is lenient, and it hides the conversion from review. *Check:* Look for stream readers and writers, `File` text methods, content helpers and `Results`/`TypedResults` `Content`/`Text` calls that have no encoding argument, in test hosts as well as production code. *Note:* The maintainer confirmed that the `Results.Content`/`Text` requirement also covers test hosts. `HttpResponse.WriteAsync(string)` is exempt (see below). <sub>Identity ADR-1266; Identity outcomes of #590</sub>
- **Don't report `HttpResponse.WriteAsync(string)` as a missing-encoding or lenient-encoding violation.** It is allowed on purpose: the ASP.NET Core request-delegate generator emits it, so banning it would break generated code. *Check:* Before you report a missing encoding, check whether the call is `HttpResponse.WriteAsync(string)`. If it is, don't report it. <sub>Identity ADR-1266</sub>
- **Don't require a throwing UTF-8 encoding when test code reads committed fixture files. The strict-decoding rule is for untrusted bytes.** Committed fixtures are trusted and don't change. A corrupted fixture still fails loudly, because its signatures, hashes or JSON no longer verify. *Check:* Before you report a lenient encoding, check whether the bytes come from an untrusted source or from a committed fixture. Report only the untrusted case. <sub>Randomness outcomes of #13</sub>
- **Compute a CSP script hash, or any hash or signature over text, from that text's UTF-8 bytes produced by a strict (throwing) UTF-8 encoding, not by `Encoding.UTF8`.** The hash has to match the exact bytes the consumer sees. `Encoding.UTF8` quietly replaces invalid characters, so the hash would cover different content. *Check:* Look for SHA-256 or hash-source code that calls `Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes` on the text being hashed. <sub>Identity ADR-1256</sub>
- **In production code, decode base64url with the strict decoder in `NCode.Base64Url`, through one shared helper where the codebase has one. Don't use `Convert.FromBase64String`, a lenient decoder or a decoder written by hand. Size the destination with `Base64Url.GetByteCountForDecode`, for example in a buffer rented from `NCode.Buffers`, and don't slice the result by `bytesWritten`.** The strict decoder rejects padding and illegal characters and throws on invalid input, so a decode that succeeds fills the buffer exactly. With one shared decoder, every caller fails in the same way. *Check:* Look for `Convert.FromBase64String` or a hand-written decoder used on base64url data, for decode buffers that are allocated too large and then sliced by `bytesWritten`, and for malformed input surfacing as different exception types across implementations. *Note:* For stored ciphertext, one source has empty or invalid text throw `CryptographicException` and a destination that is too short throw `ArgumentException`. Follow the repository's shared helper for which exceptions to throw. <sub>Identity ADR-1260; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Match opaque keys whose case matters, such as base64url ids, hashes and tokens, ordinally and exactly as written. Case-fold only values that are defined to match without regard to case.** Case-folding an opaque key produces false matches between keys that are different. *Check:* Look for `OrdinalIgnoreCase`, `ToLower`/`ToUpper` or culture-aware comparisons applied to ids, hashes or tokens. *Applies to:* `**/*.cs` <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **Format and parse values meant for machines (protocol fields, persisted data, keys, request paths) with `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture` and an exact `NumberStyles` such as `Integer` or `Float`. Never use `NumberStyles.Any`.** Culture-dependent or permissive formatting and parsing produce or accept the wrong values, such as "1,000" or a locale's decimal comma. *Check:* Look for `Parse`, `TryParse` or `ToString`, and for numeric interpolation into machine-read strings, without the invariant culture, and for any use of `NumberStyles.Any`. *Applies to:* `**/*.cs` <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **In production code, give a typed `Claim` its value in the lexical form of its declared XML Schema type, and format numbers with `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture`, for example `value.ToString(CultureInfo.InvariantCulture)`.** Mapping claims to JSON parses each value strictly by its declared type. A culture-formatted value such as "1,000" falls outside that lexical form, so it goes out as a string instead of a number. *Check:* Look for `new Claim(..., x.ToString(), ClaimValueTypes.Integer...)`, or for numeric interpolation into a typed claim's value without the invariant culture. <sub>Identity ADR-1122; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **In production code, turn date or time text into a CLR value only through the codebase's shared date-coercion helper, and only where the value is declared to be a date. That policy parses with the invariant culture into `DateTimeOffset`, treats a value without a zone as UTC, keeps an explicit offset, and fails on an out-of-range instant. Don't write your own `DateTime(Offset).Parse`/`TryParse`/`ParseExact`, and never parse a string just to test whether it looks like a date.** Hand-written parsing drifts away from the shared policy. `DateTime` parsing clamps an out-of-range instant such as `0001-01-01T00:00:00+05:00` to a machine-local value instead of failing. Sniffing turns strings such as "1.2" or "10:30" into dates and rewrites them. *Check:* Look for new `DateTime.Parse`/`TryParse`, `DateTimeOffset.TryParse` or `ParseExact` calls on date text where a shared helper exists, for `DateTime` parsing of timestamps that have no zone or carry an offset, for missing UTC handling of values without a zone, and for date parsing applied to untyped strings or claims. <sub>Identity ADR-1122; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **Count a password's length in Unicode code points (runes, as from `EnumerateRunes()`) of its NFC-normalized form, check blocklists against the NFC form, and never truncate the password. Callers pass the password to the policy exactly as submitted.** NIST SP 800-63B-4 counts each code point as one character, so a surrogate pair is one character. The length must also match what the store hashes, or a decomposed spelling passes as long enough or gets past a blocklist that lists the composed spelling. Truncation weakens the password. *Check:* Look for password length checks that use `.Length` or UTF-16 units, or that measure the text before normalization, for blocklist lookups on the submitted form, for callers that normalize before calling the policy, and for code that truncates or takes a substring of a password. <sub>Identity ADR-1236; Identity ADR-1238</sub>
- **To add query parameters to an endpoint URL, percent-encode each name and value with `Uri.EscapeDataString`, and join with `?`, or with `&` when the URL already has a query.** This follows RFC 3986 and keeps any query the endpoint already has. *Check:* Look for query strings built by concatenation without `Uri.EscapeDataString`, or for code that always adds `?` even though the URL may already have a query. <sub>Identity ADR-1285</sub>
- **In front-end code, encode an identifier placed in a URL path as a single segment with `encodeURIComponent`, and decode it with `decodeURIComponent` when parsing. Treat a blank id or a malformed encoding as matching no route.** Identifiers can contain any character, so they must survive the round trip, and invalid input must not resolve to a route. *Check:* Look for ids interpolated into paths without `encodeURIComponent`, for parsing that skips `decodeURIComponent` or doesn't catch its exception, and for blank ids that are still accepted. <sub>Identity ADR-1255</sub>
- **When writing a configured URL into output such as an HTML `href` or a response, write the configured string once it has been validated. Use the parsed `Uri` only to validate it and to derive values such as its origin, never write its `AbsoluteUri` or `ToString()`.** `Uri` normalizes the value: it adds a trailing slash and can change case and escaping. The output would then differ, byte for byte, from what was configured. *Check:* Look for `uri.AbsoluteUri` or `uri.ToString()` written into markup or responses where the original configured string is available. <sub>Identity outcomes of #747</sub>
- **Code that scans Markdown line by line for headings or markers must track fenced code blocks and skip lines inside them. A fence opens on three or more backticks or tildes, closes only on a bare run of the same character that is at least as long as the opening run, and runs to the end of the file if it is never closed.** Otherwise a matching line inside a code sample cuts the result short or corrupts it. Likewise, a single flag that flips on any fence marker makes mixed fences count headings inside code samples, or skip real headings that come after them. *Check:* Look for Markdown heading parsing with no fence tracking, or with fence detection that flips one flag on any ``` or ~~~ line, ignores the length or character of the opening run, or ignores text after the closing run. <sub>Buffers outcomes of #80; project-template outcomes of #142</sub>
- **In a regular expression meant to match within a single line, use `[ \t]` and `[^\r\n]` instead of `\s` and `.` wherever a newline must not match.** `\s` matches a newline, and `.` can too depending on the options, so input with several lines can match a pattern meant for one line. *Check:* Look for single-line patterns that use `\s` between tokens, or `.*`, where the input may contain line breaks and the options aren't stated. <sub>project-template outcomes of #146</sub>
- **When parsing `Accept-Language` into locale preferences, sort the entries by quality, highest first, and drop the `*` wildcard and any entry with a quality of zero.** The user agent's preferences have to be read in the priority it states, and neither q=0 nor the wildcard names a language to render. *Check:* Look for `Accept-Language` parsing that keeps header order regardless of q-values, or that passes `*` or q=0 entries on as preferences. <sub>Identity ADR-1402</sub>
- **Server-rendered pages write the selected locale's tag into the `lang` attribute of the `html` element. Client-side code on those pages renders in that document language instead of choosing its own from `navigator.languages`.** If the client chose on its own, pages without JavaScript would stay in one language, the first frame would flash another, and the document's `lang` wouldn't match the text the user reads. *Check:* Look for rendered HTML documents with no `lang` set by the server, or for front-end code that takes its locale from `navigator.language(s)` instead of the document's `lang`. <sub>Identity ADR-1402</sub>
- **Format values that can come out differently by culture (negative or fractional numbers, dates, numbers joined with `string.Join`) with `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture` in diagnostic, failure and validation messages.** Otherwise the same report reads differently in different cultures, for example with a different negative sign or decimal separator. *Check:* Look for `string.Join` over numeric collections, and for interpolation of signed, fractional or date values, without the invariant culture in code that builds messages. *Note:* One source (an ADR on validation messages) asks for invariant formatting of every interpolated value in violation descriptions. The more recent review outcomes don't flag non-negative integers or `TimeSpan` values in their default format, because those print the same in every culture (see the next rule). <sub>coordination outcomes of #21; Identity ADR-1206</sub>
- **Don't ask for `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture` or `FormattableString.Invariant` in exception, log or validation messages meant for people when the only interpolated values are non-negative integers or `TimeSpan` values in their default format. The invariant-culture rule covers values meant for machines.** These values print the same in every .NET culture (plain digits, no group separator), CA1305 accepts them, and the message is read by a person. *Check:* Before you report culture-sensitive formatting, check whether a machine reads the string (protocol, persisted or parsed data, a key, a request path) and whether the interpolated values could format differently by culture. Report only machine-read strings, or values whose format depends on culture. <sub>Randomness outcomes of #12; Randomness outcomes of #13; Randomness outcomes of #18; coordination outcomes of #14; coordination outcomes of #17; coordination outcomes of #31; coordination outcomes of #32</sub>
- **Write a non-ASCII character in a C# string or `u8` literal as a Unicode escape (`\uXXXX`) whenever the exact code points or bytes matter, for example `"caf\u00e9"` rather than a pasted `é`. In tests about normalization, cover both the precomposed (`"café"`) and decomposed (`"café"`) forms.** An editor may normalize a pasted character without telling you, which changes the bytes and makes the test check a different sequence from the one it claims to. *Check:* Look for raw accented, combining or other non-ASCII characters in string literals, especially in test data that depends on encoding or normalization. <sub>Buffers outcomes of #80; Identity csharp-testing.instructions.md; Identity csharp-tests.instructions.md; coordination outcomes of #17</sub>
- **Use `u8` string literals for bytes that hold valid UTF-8 text. Declare a fixed protocol label (an HKDF info, purpose or prefix) as a `ReadOnlySpan<byte>` property that returns a `u8` literal. Write explicit byte arrays only for invalid UTF-8 or error cases.** `u8` literals are clearer, cost nothing per call and pass straight to span APIs, whereas a `const string` is encoded again on every call. *Check:* Look for `Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("literal")`, for constant strings encoded before use in crypto or wire formats, and for hand-written byte arrays that spell out valid text. <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity review of #420</sub>
- **Save new files as UTF-8 without a byte-order mark and with LF line endings, following the repository's `.editorconfig`. This includes files generated by tools such as `dotnet ef migrations add`. When editing an existing file, keep its encoding and BOM as they are, for example the UTF-8 BOM on a Visual Studio `.sln`, unless the change is meant to convert the file.** UTF-8 without a BOM and LF is the base file convention. Adding or removing a BOM as a side effect changes the file's encoding, adds noise to the diff, and invites the IDE to flip it back on its next save. *Check:* Look for added files that start with U+FEFF or use CRLF line endings, including newly scaffolded migration, designer and snapshot files, and for edited files whose only first-line change is a BOM added or removed without the PR saying it changes the encoding. *Note:* Generic rules say every file is UTF-8 without a BOM. The more specific outcome on editing existing IDE-managed files says to keep an existing BOM, so this rule keeps an existing file's encoding. <sub>Identity project-template.instructions.md; identity-platform project-template.instructions.md; Identity outcomes of #598; NCode.Disposables outcomes of #33; Identity ADR-1180</sub>
- **In new code, parse JSON with `JsonElement.Parse` instead of `JsonDocument.Parse` or `JsonDocument.ParseValue` wherever an element is all that's needed.** `JsonElement.Parse` leaves no disposable document for anyone to own or forget to dispose, and the maintainer is moving off the older parsing APIs. *Check:* Look for new `JsonDocument.Parse` or `JsonDocument.ParseValue` calls where `JsonElement.Parse` would do. <sub>Identity review of #382</sub>
